title: Driver / Operator — Pumper
summary: Safe apparatus operation, placement, water supply, pump systems, hydraulics, troubleshooting, and fireground communication as one integrated role.

skills.title: Hydrant Operations
skills.summary: Connect a reliable hydrant supply, manage intake pressure, watch residual, and communicate before changing demand.
skills.whyItMatters: Most urban structure fires succeed or fail on whether the first engine actually has the water the fire needs. Hydrant work is not just hooking a hose — it is reading the system while the incident changes.
learningPoints: A hydrant is a connection to a water system with limits. Static pressure is not available flow.
Residual pressure is the best early warning that the system is being asked for more than it can comfortably give.
Intake pressure, gated intake control, and valve speed protect the pump, the water main, and the people on the lines.
Communicate before opening additional lines, starting a master stream, or making a large change in supply.
Department SOP, hydrant wrench/adapter package, and local water-system quirks beat any generic sequence.
beforeYouDo: Know which hydrant is the assigned source and whether it is on the same main as nearby hydrants.
Confirm the apparatus intake, gated valve, LDH/supply hose, and steamer/outlet adapters for this engine.
Agree who works the hydrant, who watches the panel, and how you will say “hold,” “open,” and “shut down.”

terminology.meaning: Hydrant/system pressure with no fire-department flow yet.
Pressure remaining while water is flowing. A falling residual means demand is catching up to supply.
What the pump is seeing on the supply side. Watch it as lines open.
The large hydrant outlet usually used for LDH supply.
Control water into the pump instead of slamming the system open or shut.

safetyNotes: Never straddle hose that may charge. Charge and valve movement can injure.
Open and close hydrant valves slowly to limit water-hammer and main damage.
Do not assume a charged supply line is a completed water supply. Confirm intake and residual.
If residual is falling hard, do not add large additional demand until supply is improved or attack is adjusted.
Follow department traffic, hydrant-location, and apparatus-placement rules. The hydrant firefighter is in the street.

practiceResources.label: Hydrant Flow Calculator
practiceResources.note: Estimate available flow from test data.

practiceResources.label: Pump Pressure Calculator
practiceResources.note: Connect supply decisions to discharge pressure.

drill.objective: Establish hydrant-to-engine water, monitor residual/intake, and communicate before changing demand.
drill.equipment: Engine, hydrant kit, supply hose/LDH, hydrant wrench, gated intake as equipped, radios.
drill.setup: Use an approved hydrant or a training hydrant/sim. Brief roles: hydrant firefighter, pump operator, officer. State the objective and the stop signal.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: Walk the hydrant connection and communication sequence without charging if water is not available. Name who talks, what is confirmed, and what “open it” actually means for your department.
commonMistakes: No confirmation that water is at the pump
Vague ‘you got it’ instead of a clear report
debrief: What is the first thing the pump operator should see after the hydrant is opened?
When would we not open a second large discharge?

15.title: 15-minute supply evolution
15.instructions: Deploy the supply line, make the hydrant, establish water to the engine, and place one attack line in service. Operator reports static, residual, and intake. Then add or shut a second line and report what changed.
commonMistakes: No one watching residual when the second line opens
debrief: What did residual do when the second line opened?
What would you do if residual dropped below your department’s comfort number?

30.title: 30-minute company scenario
30.instructions: Run an engine-company scenario with changing fire flow: initial attack line, second line, then a high-flow request (deck gun or two more lines — tabletop the high flow if the site cannot support it). Operator must keep a water-supply picture and say when the system is approaching its limit. Include a communication failure and a kink/intake problem to troubleshoot.
performancePoints: Placement supports supply and later units
Crew told before major water changes
commonMistakes: Treating hydrant connection as ‘done’ and walking away
Adding a master stream on a weak residual
No plan if this hydrant is a dog
debrief: When should we take a second hydrant or start a relay?
Who owns the decision to refuse additional flow?

readinessQuestions.q: A residual pressure that is falling while you add lines most likely means:
choices: The pump is overheating
The water system is approaching the flow it can give at that hydrant
The attack line nozzle is too small
The hydrant is a dry barrel and cannot be used
readinessQuestions.why: Residual is the live picture of remaining system capacity. Falling residual while demand rises is the warning to stop adding large flow or improve supply.

readinessQuestions.q: Before making a major change in water supply or adding a large discharge, the operator should:
choices: Wait until someone complains about low pressure
Communicate the change and check intake/residual
Open every gated intake at once
Increase RPM first, then look at gauges
readinessQuestions.why: People on the line, later-arriving apparatus, and the water system all need a heads-up. Look at supply gauges, then act.

readinessQuestions.q: Which sign suggests the water system is approaching available flow?
choices: Rising residual with stable RPM
Intake climbing with no discharge open
Rapidly falling residual, hunting intake, or cavitation signs as flow increases
A warm pump panel in cold weather
readinessQuestions.why: The system tells you through residual, intake, and pump noise/feel. Do not wait for a line to go flat.

readinessQuestions.q: Hydrant valves should generally be operated:
choices: As fast as possible to get water
Slowly, to limit water hammer and control intake
Only by the officer
Only after the fire is knocked down
readinessQuestions.why: Controlled valve movement protects mains, hydrants, hose, and the pump.

skills.title: Pump Theory
skills.summary: Understand how a centrifugal fire pump makes pressure, why it needs water at the eye of the impeller, and what gauges are telling you.
skills.whyItMatters: Formulas fail in the street if the operator does not know what the machine is doing. Pump theory is how you recognize cavitation, loss of prime, and useless RPM.
learningPoints: A centrifugal pump moves water with an impeller. It does not ‘suck’ well if air is in the impeller eye.
Net pump pressure is about the work the pump is doing between intake and discharge — not a single magic number on one gauge.
Cavitation is water turning to vapor at the impeller because intake conditions cannot feed the pump. It damages the pump and starves lines.
Priming is for drafting/air at the impeller. A pressurized hydrant supply is a different problem than a dry pump.
Manufacturer and department pump-mode procedures (transfer valve, pressure/volume, governor/relief) outrank generic diagrams.
beforeYouDo: Identify transfer valve, primer, intake, tank-to-pump, and governor/relief on THIS apparatus.
Know whether you are on tank, hydrant, or draft before changing RPM.

terminology.meaning: Rotating component that adds energy to the water.
Removing air so the impeller is water-filled and can pump.
Vapor bubbles forming and collapsing at the impeller from inadequate intake conditions.
How some two-stage pumps are set for higher pressure or higher volume.

safetyNotes: Do not run a dry pump. Follow apparatus limits for tank water and primer use.
Unusual noise, vibration, or a discharge gauge that will not rise with RPM is a stop-and-diagnose cue.

practiceResources.label: Pumper Flashcards
practiceResources.note: Active recall on pump and hydraulics terms.

drill.objective: Explain pump mode, priming, and cavitation signs on the assigned apparatus, then diagnose two common failures.
drill.equipment: Assigned pumper (or pump panel trainer), department pump chart, radios.
drill.setup: Walk around the panel. No live pumping required for the 5-minute version. Use tank water only if authorized.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: Point to primer, tank-to-pump, intakes, transfer valve, and governor/relief. State when each is used.
commonMistakes: Priming on a hydrant supply by habit
debrief: When do we prime? When do we not?

15.title: 15-minute panel talk-through
15.instructions: Give three conditions: tank water to a preconnect, hydrant supply, then a noisy pump with falling intake. Operator states actions in order.
commonMistakes: Revving the engine to ‘make pressure’ with no water
debrief: What would you tell the officer?

30.title: 30-minute diagnosis drill
30.instructions: Run or tabletop: loss of prime, gated intake left closed, and a weak hydrant. Operator must change one variable at a time.
debrief: Which clue separated cavitation from a closed valve?

readinessQuestions.q: A centrifugal fire pump generally needs which condition at the impeller to work?
choices: Air in the impeller eye
Water filling the impeller
The relief valve fully open
The parking brake released
readinessQuestions.why: No water at the impeller means no reliable pumping. That is why prime and intake matter.

readinessQuestions.q: Cavitation is best understood as:
choices: Too much foam in the tank
Vapor forming at the impeller because the pump is being asked for more than intake can supply
A hydrant that is a wet barrel
Normal governor hunting
readinessQuestions.why: Fix supply/intake or reduce demand. More RPM often makes cavitation worse.

readinessQuestions.q: Priming is typically associated with:
choices: A charged hydrant supply that already fills the pump
Removing air so a dry or drafting pump can move water
Setting the aerial outriggers
Opening the tank fill
readinessQuestions.why: Do not treat priming as a generic ‘start the pump’ step on a pressurized supply unless your apparatus procedure says so.

officialSources.label: Apparatus manufacturer pump manual
officialSources.scope: Pump mode, primer, and cavitation limits are apparatus-specific.

skills.title: Daily Apparatus Inspection
skills.summary: Find the problem in the bay, not on the fireground. Fluids, warning systems, pump, tires, equipment, and documentation.
skills.whyItMatters: Most ‘it died on the call’ stories started as a skipped check. Inspection is an operator skill, not busywork.
learningPoints: Use the department sheet as the legal/operational checklist.
Look, listen, feel, and function-test what policy allows.
Out-of-service criteria must be known before you need them.
Document defects. A verbal ‘it’s fine’ is not a record.
beforeYouDo: Get the department inspection form for this apparatus.
Know who you notify for a defect and what takes the rig out of service.

terminology.meaning: Out of service — the apparatus or a system cannot be safely used.
Some defects are noted and monitored; others park the rig. Policy decides.

safetyNotes: Chock, park brake, and exhaust/CO awareness in the bay.
Do not disable warning systems to ‘pass’ a check.
High-voltage hybrid/electric apparatus follow manufacturer rules.

drill.objective: Complete a documented daily check emphasizing pump, water, warning systems, and equipment readiness.
drill.equipment: Assigned apparatus, department inspection sheet, flashlight, PPE as required.
drill.setup: Start from a known ‘ready’ or intentionally seeded training defect if the training officer allows.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: List the five things that would park THIS rig this morning.
debrief: What is our notification path?

15.title: 15-minute walk-around
15.instructions: Run the department sheet. Report one finding, even if ‘no defects.’
debrief: What did you actually function-test?

30.title: 30-minute readiness drill
30.instructions: Full check plus a ‘missing tool / low oil / inop warning light’ inject. Crew restores or correctly OOS’s the unit.
commonMistakes: Hiding a defect to stay in service
debrief: Who has authority to OOS?

readinessQuestions.q: The primary checklist for a daily apparatus inspection is:
choices: A generic social-media list
The department form plus manufacturer/out-of-service rules
Whatever the last driver remembered
Only the pump panel
readinessQuestions.why: Liability and readiness live on the department sheet.

readinessQuestions.q: A warning-system defect should be:
choices: Ignored if the engine starts
Documented and handled per OOS/notification policy
Reset by pulling a fuse
Left for the next shift without comment
readinessQuestions.why: Warning systems are how the public and the crew get a chance to see you.

readinessQuestions.q: Why document a minor deficiency that does not OOS the rig?
choices: To fill the log
So the next operator and maintenance see the trend before it fails on a call
It is not necessary
Only if an officer asks
readinessQuestions.why: Trends are how pumps, tires, and governors fail ‘suddenly.’

officialSources.label: National Fire Academy
officialSources.scope: Free federal fire-service training and professional development

officialSources.label: Department inspection SOP and manufacturer manual
officialSources.scope: Inspection content and OOS criteria are local and apparatus-specific.

skills.title: Engage Pump
skills.summary: Position, shift to pump, confirm pump mode, tank-to-pump or supply, and a charged first line without guessing.
skills.whyItMatters: The first 60 seconds of pumping set up everything that follows. A missed shift confirmation is a dry line at the door.
learningPoints: Follow the exact manufacturer/department sequence for THIS transmission and pump.
Confirm pump mode with indicators, not hope.
Know whether the first water is tank or hydrant.
Set a pressure control device before the line gets away from you.
beforeYouDo: Spot the apparatus so pump panel, intakes, and later units can work.
Know the first-line package (length, GPM, nozzle pressure).

terminology.meaning: Transferring driveline power to the fire pump per apparatus design.
Onboard water feeding the pump until a supply is established.

safetyNotes: Parking brake and wheel chocks per SOP before pumping.
Do not leave the cab until the shift is confirmed if that is your procedure.
Watch for open discharges and personnel in front of lines.

drill.objective: Engage the pump per department procedure and place the standard first line in service with a pressure-control setting.
drill.equipment: Assigned pumper, attack line, water source authorized for training.
drill.setup: Chocks, radio, and a safety officer. Use tank water only if the site and policy allow.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: Say the engage-pump sequence out loud, including confirmation cues.
commonMistakes: Assuming the light means water is at the nozzle
debrief: What tells you the pump is actually in pump?

15.title: 15-minute first line
15.instructions: Engage pump, tank-to-pump, charge the standard preconnect, set governor/relief, report pressures.
commonMistakes: Charging before the nozzle firefighter is ready
debrief: What pressure did you choose and why?

30.title: 30-minute transition
30.instructions: First line on tank, then transition to hydrant without losing the line. Include a failed pump-shift inject if training-safe.
commonMistakes: Dumping the tank with no supply plan
debrief: When do we leave tank water and why?

readinessQuestions.q: The safest way to know the pump is engaged is:
choices: The parking brake is set
Follow apparatus indicators/procedure, not assumption
The siren still works
Someone yelled ‘pump’
readinessQuestions.why: Each apparatus has confirmation cues. Learn them.

readinessQuestions.q: Pressure control (governor/relief) should be:
choices: Set after a line already surged
Part of placing the first line in service
Only used on relays
Left off so you can ‘feel’ the pump
readinessQuestions.why: It is how you keep a firefighter from being launched by a sudden pressure spike.

readinessQuestions.q: Tank-to-pump is used to:
choices: Fill the booster tank from a hydrant only
Supply the pump from onboard water until a source is established
Prime a hydrant
Cool the transmission
readinessQuestions.why: Have a supply plan before the tank is gone.

officialSources.scope: Free federal fire-service training and professional development

officialSources.label: Apparatus manufacturer operating instructions
officialSources.scope: Pump-shift steps differ by make, model, and transmission.

skills.title: Friction Loss and PDP
skills.summary: Estimate pump discharge pressure from nozzle pressure, hose friction, elevation, and appliances — then sanity-check the number.
skills.whyItMatters: A wrong PDP either starves the nozzle or overpressures people and hose. The math is a starting point; the gauges and the nozzle firefighter tell you if it is working.
learningPoints: PDP ≈ NP + FL + elevation + appliance (department formula may vary).
Friction loss rises with flow and length and depends on hose diameter/C-value.
Your department hose/nozzle package matters more than a textbook example.
If the number does not match what the gauges and the line are doing, believe the fireground.
beforeYouDo: Know the target NP and GPM for the line you are pumping.
Know department C-values or pump chart for assigned hose.

terminology.meaning: Pump discharge pressure — what you are trying to produce for that line.
Friction loss in the hose/appliances between pump and nozzle/device.
Coefficient used in common training formulas for a hose diameter at a given flow.

safetyNotes: Do not chase a formula into an unsafe pressure.
Elevation and long lays change everything — re-calculate when the layout changes.

seeResources.label: Friction Loss Calculator
seeResources.note: Work FL from flow, length, and C.

seeResources.label: Friction Loss Table
seeResources.note: See how diameter and flow change FL.

drill.objective: Calculate PDP for the department’s standard lines, then compare the estimate to a pump-chart or instructor target.
drill.equipment: Calculator or pump chart, sample hose layouts, radios optional.
drill.setup: Classroom or bay. Use actual department line packages, not random textbook numbers.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: Compute PDP for the standard 1¾ preconnect. Say each component.
debrief: What would 100 more feet do?

15.title: 15-minute chart vs calc
15.instructions: Three layouts: preconnect, 2½, and a long lay. Compare calculator to department chart.
commonMistakes: Mixing diameters in one formula blindly
debrief: When do we trust the chart over the calculator?

30.title: 30-minute live or tabletop pump
30.instructions: Pump a training line if authorized; otherwise tabletop gauge pictures. Match PDP to nozzle performance and adjust.
commonMistakes: Never looking at the gauge after the math
debrief: What told you the formula was off?

readinessQuestions.q: If hose length doubles and flow stays the same, friction loss generally:
choices: Stays the same
Approximately doubles
Drops by half
Depends only on RPM
readinessQuestions.why: FL is proportional to length in the common training model.

readinessQuestions.q: A calculated PDP is:
choices: An official required discharge pressure
A training estimate to be checked against gauges, nozzle, and SOP
Always higher than 200 psi
Only for relay pumping
readinessQuestions.why: FireOpsSim calculators are training tools, not policy.

readinessQuestions.q: Increasing GPM on the same hose will generally:
choices: Lower friction loss
Raise friction loss sharply
Never affect PDP
Only affect elevation
readinessQuestions.why: Flow has a large effect (often modeled with a square relationship).

officialSources.label: National Fire Academy
officialSources.scope: Free federal fire-service training and professional development

officialSources.label: Department pump chart / hose-nozzle package
officialSources.scope: Operational target pressures come from the AHJ and the hose you actually carry.

skills.title: Multiple Attack Lines
skills.summary: Keep pressure, supply, and communication stable when a second or third line opens or shuts.
skills.whyItMatters: The fire does not wait while you re-do math. Opening another line changes flow, residual, and every existing discharge.
learningPoints: Each additional line is more GPM from the same pump and the same water system.
Tell the officer and the lines before you change a lot of water.
Watch residual and intake as much as discharge.
Know which line is which on the panel.
beforeYouDo: Know estimated GPM of each line in service.
Have supply established or a tank plan that can survive the extra line.

terminology.meaning: A gated outlet on the pump panel feeding a specific line or device.
Can hold pressure as flow changes — still watch supply.

safetyNotes: A sudden shut-down of one line can spike pressure on another if pressure control is wrong or off.
Do not steal the attack line’s water to feed a vanity layout.

drill.objective: Place two attack lines in service, report what residual/intake did, then shut one down without surprising the remaining line.
drill.equipment: Pumper, two attack lines, authorized water, radios.
drill.setup: Brief who calls for the second line and how the operator acknowledges.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: Talk through adding a second line: supply check, communication, then open.
debrief: What do we tell the first nozzle?

15.title: 15-minute two-line pump
15.instructions: One line, then second line, then one shutdown. Operator reports gauges each time.
debrief: Which gauge moved first?

30.title: 30-minute fire-flow scenario
30.instructions: Changing request: second line, then a third or a high-flow device (tabletop if needed). Operator must say when supply cannot support it.
commonMistakes: Silent panel while the fire grows
debrief: What is our next water move?

readinessQuestions.q: When a second attack line opens, the operator should first be thinking about:
choices: Siren use
Additional flow vs remaining supply and existing line pressures
Only foam
Turning off the first line automatically
readinessQuestions.why: Flow has to come from somewhere.

readinessQuestions.q: Shutting down one of two lines can:
choices: Never affect the other line
Spike pressure on the remaining line if pressure control is not managing it
Always drop residual
Prime the pump
readinessQuestions.why: Pressure control and communication exist for this moment.

readinessQuestions.q: The officer asks for a third line while residual is already falling. Best operator action:
choices: Open it immediately to be a team player
Report the supply picture and the risk, then follow the officer’s informed decision / improve supply
Leave the panel to pull the line
Increase RPM only
readinessQuestions.why: Give the officer the water facts. Do not silently exceed the system.

officialSources.label: National Fire Academy
officialSources.scope: Free federal fire-service training and professional development

officialSources.label: Department pumping SOP
officialSources.scope: Line designations, color codes, and target pressures are local.

skills.title: Master Stream Operations
skills.summary: High-flow devices need water, reaction awareness, supply, and a reason — not just a bigger nozzle.
skills.whyItMatters: A master stream can overwhelm a hydrant, a pump, and a building. It is a tactical tool with a supply problem attached.
learningPoints: Know the device GPM and NP before you open it.
Confirm supply can support that flow.
Reaction, collapse, and stream direction are safety problems, not decorations.
Transitioning to or from handlines changes everything on the panel.
beforeYouDo: Estimate needed flow vs hydrant/tank reality.
Know whether this is deck gun, portable monitor, or aerial waterway — they are not the same.

terminology.meaning: High-capacity stream from a monitor, deck gun, or waterway — typically hundreds of GPM.
Force trying to push the device/apparatus.

safetyNotes: Do not staff an unsafe portable monitor.
Watch collapse zones and electrical hazards.
Do not take the handline’s last water to feed a gun without a plan.

practiceResources.label: Hydrant Flow Calculator
practiceResources.note: Can this hydrant support the gun?

drill.objective: Decide whether a master stream is supply-supported, then tabletop or flow a training stream if authorized.
drill.equipment: Flow data, calculators, apparatus if authorized, radios.
drill.setup: If you cannot flow a gun, tabletop the numbers and the placement.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: Name GPM, supply need, and one reason you would refuse the gun.
debrief: What hydrant picture do we need first?

15.title: 15-minute calc + placement
15.instructions: Work a 500–1000 GPM request against a hydrant estimate. Place the rig for later units.
debrief: If residual is 25 psi while flowing 250, do we add 750?

30.title: 30-minute evolution
30.instructions: Authorized flow or full tabletop: handline, then gun request, then back. Operator keeps a water narrative.
debrief: When does the gun become a liability?

readinessQuestions.q: Before opening a master stream, the operator needs:
choices: Only the officer’s enthusiasm
A flow target, a supply that can support it, and a safe device/crew setup
The tank fill open
Foam in every case
readinessQuestions.why: High flow without supply is a show, then a failure.

readinessQuestions.q: A portable monitor should be:
choices: Staffed in the collapse zone to ‘aim better’
Set and operated per department/manufacturer rules, with reaction considered
Supplied by a garden hose
Opened before the supply line is charged
readinessQuestions.why: Uncontrolled reaction injures people.

readinessQuestions.q: If residual collapses when the gun opens, you should:
choices: Keep it open to ‘win’
Reduce demand and/or improve supply and tell command
Close the hydrant completely
Switch to tank water only and hope
readinessQuestions.why: Give command the water facts immediately.

officialSources.label: National Fire Academy
officialSources.scope: Free federal fire-service training and professional development

officialSources.label: Device and apparatus manufacturer instructions
officialSources.scope: Flow, NP, and reaction limits are equipment-specific.

skills.title: Relay Pumping
skills.summary: Move water a long distance with more than one pump: roles, intake targets, communications, and failure recognition.
skills.whyItMatters: Relays fail from silence and ego, not from math. Every engine needs a role, an intake target, and a way to say ‘hold.’
learningPoints: Source, relay, and attack pumpers have different jobs.
Intake pressure at the next engine is the product, not dump pressure for sport.
Talk before you change RPM a lot.
Plan for a burst, a kink, or a dropped hydrant.
beforeYouDo: Know LDH diameter, lay length, and target flow.
Assign radio words for increase/decrease/hold.

terminology.meaning: The engine at the water source.
Boosts pressure in the supply line toward the fire.
The engine supplying fire streams.

safetyNotes: Do not overpressure LDH.
Traffic and hose crossings on long lays.
Never assume the next engine saw your gauge.

drill.objective: Assign source/relay/attack roles, set an intake target, and practice the communication loop for a pressure change.
drill.equipment: Map or cones, radios, calculators, two or more engines if available — otherwise tabletop.
drill.setup: Even a tabletop with three people works: source, relay, attack.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: Name the three roles and one radio phrase for ‘hold.’
commonMistakes: Everyone pumping ‘as hard as they can’
debrief: Who owns intake at the attack engine?

15.title: 15-minute tabletop relay
15.instructions: Given a long lay and a flow, pick spacing with the calculator and brief the comms plan.
debrief: What if the middle engine dies?

30.title: 30-minute evolution or full tabletop
30.instructions: Change flow twice. Each pumper reports intake/discharge. Inject a kink or lost source.
debrief: What would make you abort the relay?

readinessQuestions.q: The attack pumper in a relay primarily cares about:
choices: How impressive the source RPM looks
Stable intake and enough flow for the fire streams
Closing all discharges
Drafting on a hydrant
readinessQuestions.why: Intake at the fire engine is the point of the relay.

readinessQuestions.q: Before increasing RPM significantly in a relay, operators should:
choices: Wait 10 minutes
Communicate the change so the next engine is not surprised
Shut the hydrant
Switch to tank water
readinessQuestions.why: Silence creates overpressure and cavitation.

readinessQuestions.q: A relay is a good tool when:
choices: The fire is small and a preconnect would do
The source is far and one engine cannot deliver the needed flow/pressure alone
You want to avoid hydrants in town
The officer is not on scene
readinessQuestions.why: Match the water method to the distance and demand.

officialSources.label: National Fire Academy
officialSources.scope: Free federal fire-service training and professional development

officialSources.label: Department LDH / relay SOP
officialSources.scope: Hose ratings, intake targets, and engine spacing are AHJ-specific.

skills.title: Drafting
skills.summary: Build an airtight suction path, prime, lift water from a static source, and recognize cavitation and air leaks.
skills.whyItMatters: Drafting is unforgiving. One air leak or a fouled strainer turns a rural fire into a tank of regrets.
learningPoints: Hard suction must be airtight. Connections and gaskets matter.
Lift, strainer placement, and primer use follow physics and the manual.
Watch intake: vacuum that is too high is a warning.
Have a plan for a lost prime during pumping.
beforeYouDo: Site the engine for lift, hose, and later tenders if used.
Inspect gaskets and strainer before you need them.

terminology.meaning: Vertical distance from water surface to the pump.
Keeps debris out of the suction hose; must stay submerged and unobstructed.
Intake-side reading while drafting.

safetyNotes: Drowning, drop-offs, and ice at static sources.
Carbon monoxide if idling in a hole or against a wall.
Do not walk the suction hose once it is under vacuum in an unsafe way.

practiceResources.note: When draft is not enough, plan rural water.

drill.objective: Set up a draft (live or walk-through), prime, and name three failure clues.
drill.equipment: Pumper, hard suction, strainer, approved static source or dry setup, PPE.
drill.setup: Use a training pond/draft pit if available. Otherwise complete a dry airtight setup and primer talk-through.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: Show gasket, strainer, and primer. State max practical lift as a concept, not a brag.
debrief: Where do air leaks hide?

15.title: 15-minute setup
15.instructions: Make all connections, strainer in water (or simulated), primer sequence verbalized, failure clues listed.
debrief: What does a rising vacuum with no water mean?

30.title: 30-minute draft evolution

readinessQuestions.q: The most common practical enemy of a draft is:
choices: Too much residual pressure
Air leaks or a strainer that cannot feed the pump
A wet-barrel hydrant
Foam
readinessQuestions.why: Air and starved intake stop centrifugal pumps.

readinessQuestions.q: Hard suction hose is used because:
choices: It looks traditional
It can handle vacuum without collapsing like soft hose
It has less friction than LDH always
It stores water
readinessQuestions.why: Soft supply hose is not a substitute for suction hose in a true draft.

readinessQuestions.q: If the pump cavitates while drafting, a useful first thought is:
choices: More RPM
Reduce demand and check lift, strainer, and air leaks
Open every discharge
Turn off the primer forever
readinessQuestions.why: Fix the intake side; do not bully the impeller.

skills.title: Standpipe and FDC Operations
skills.summary: Supply a standpipe or sprinkler FDC with the right hose, the right pressure method, and a clear communication loop with the interior crew.
skills.whyItMatters: High-rise and sprinklered buildings fail the first engine when the operator treats an FDC like a hydrant with extra hose. Elevation, system loss, and the people on the standpipe outlet all have to be in the same picture.
learningPoints: An FDC is a building fire-protection inlet. You are pushing water into a system with its own pipes, valves, and losses — not just a long attack line.
Standpipe PDP is nozzle pressure plus hose on the floor plus elevation plus system/FDC loss. Department charts and the building’s system beat a generic number.
Confirm the connection: Siamese vs storz, caps, clapper, and whether this FDC actually feeds the standpipe or sprinkler zone you think it does.
Place the engine so later trucks can still work, LDH can reach, and you are not blocking the building’s only access.
Talk to the interior/standpipe crew before large pressure changes. They feel your panel before you hear their radio.
beforeYouDo: Know this apparatus’ FDC hose, adapters, and whether you pump sprinkler and standpipe from the same inlet.
Agree who owns pressure: pump operator, officer, or the crew at the standpipe outlet.
Have a backup if the FDC is damaged, capped wrong, or the system is isolated.

terminology.meaning: Fire department connection — the inlet on the building (or nearby) where the engine supplies the system.
Fixed piping that delivers water to hose outlets on upper floors or remote areas.
Pressure lost in the building piping, valves, and connection — often a department or building-specific allowance.
Pressure needed to lift water to the fire floor. Floor count is a training estimate; the building and SOP win.
A two-inlet FDC body. Pump both sides unless the system and SOP say otherwise.

safetyNotes: Do not assume an FDC is in service. Caps, debris, a closed OS&Y, or a broken clapper can give you a beautiful discharge gauge and no water upstairs.
Overpressure can damage the system and the hose on the floor. Follow department max PDP and relief/governor practice.
LDH and charged FDC lines in a driveway are a trip and vehicle hazard. Place, chock, and light as SOP requires.
If the interior crew reports no water, treat it as a water emergency — not an argument about your math.

drill.objective: Connect and pump an FDC (live or tabletop), state the pressure method, and communicate before changing PDP.
drill.equipment: Engine, LDH/supply to FDC, adapters/caps wrench, radios, standpipe/FDC calculator or department chart, building photo or training FDC.
drill.setup: Use a training FDC or a tabletop building. Brief: operator, hydrant/supply firefighter, interior/standpipe voice. Name the stop signal and max PDP.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: Walk the FDC: caps, inlets, what it feeds, hose choice, and who talks. Name every term in the PDP stack for this building without charging if water is not available.
commonMistakes: No plan if the connection is clogged
debrief: What does this FDC actually supply?
What is the first radio sentence if upstairs reports no water?

15.title: 15-minute supply evolution
15.instructions: Make the FDC, establish supply, and set an initial PDP from the calculator or chart. Then change floors or add a second line (tabletop the second line if the site cannot support it). Operator reports PDP, intake/residual, and what changed.
commonMistakes: Pumping a number with no floor or hose story
No confirmation water is in the system
debrief: What would you do if PDP is correct and the floor still has no water?
When would you refuse a higher-pressure request?

30.title: 30-minute high-rise / sprinkler scenario
30.instructions: Run a building scenario: first connection, a clogged or one-sided FDC inject, then a floor change or sprinkler vs standpipe question. Operator must keep supply, PDP, and the interior picture together. Include a later-arriving truck that needs the spot you took.
performancePoints: Crew told before major pressure changes
commonMistakes: Blocking the aerial or the only driveway
Raising PDP instead of checking the connection
Silent panel while the standpipe crew is dry
debrief: How do we tell standpipe support from sprinkler support on this building?
Who owns the decision to abandon this FDC?

readinessQuestions.q: Pump discharge pressure for a standpipe assignment is best thought of as:
choices: Whatever residual the hydrant showed
Nozzle pressure plus hose on the fire floor plus elevation plus system/FDC loss, using the department method
Always 150 psi because that is a common classroom number
Intake pressure times two
readinessQuestions.why: Stack the pieces. The building, the hose package, and SOP decide the number — not a slogan.

readinessQuestions.q: If the interior crew reports no water at the standpipe outlet while your discharge gauge looks healthy, a useful first thought is:
choices: Tell them to open the nozzle more
Check the FDC/path into the system, valves, and whether you are actually supplying that zone
Double RPM immediately
Shut down and leave
readinessQuestions.why: A pretty panel does not prove water is in the riser. Find the break in the path.

readinessQuestions.q: Many FDCs are two-inlet bodies. Unless SOP and the system say otherwise, engines should usually:
choices: Pump one inlet so the other stays pretty
Supply both inlets
Avoid FDC work and draft from a planter
Cap both inlets after charging
readinessQuestions.why: Two inlets exist to move volume into the system and to have a backup path. Follow the local connection rule.

readinessQuestions.q: Before a large PDP increase to an FDC, the operator should:
choices: Wait until hose bursts
Tell the interior/standpipe crew and watch supply gauges
Open every discharge on the panel
Switch to tank water
readinessQuestions.why: People on the line feel your change. Supply has to support it.

skills.title: Rural Water and Tender Shuttle
skills.summary: Keep fire flow coming when there is no hydrant: tank duration, fill and dump sites, shuttle math, and the radio loop that actually delivers water.
skills.whyItMatters: Rural fires run out of water in minutes if the first engine treats tank water as infinite. Shuttle success is cycle time and jobs — not how many tenders are ‘en route.’
learningPoints: Tank duration is working water divided by flow. Reserve exists so you can still move the engine or protect a crew when the shuttle hiccups.
Sustained shuttle GPM is usable gallons per tender divided by cycle time, times the number of tenders actually completing the loop.
Cycle time is fill + travel + dump + travel + turnaround. The slowest step, not the fastest truck, sets the flow.
Fill site, dump site, nurse, and attack pumper are different jobs. Mixing them on the radio is how water stops.
Drafting, a relay, or a second fill site may beat adding another tender that has nowhere to dump.
beforeYouDo: Know this engine’s tank size, usable water, and the department reserve rule.
Name the fill site, dump method (portable tank, nurse, jet dump), and who owns traffic at each end.
Agree the radio words for ‘hold dump,’ ‘need water,’ and ‘fill site delay.’

terminology.meaning: Minutes for one tender to fill, travel, dump, return, and turn around.
Where tenders offload — portable tanks, a nurse pumper, or a jet-dump into a tank.
Hydrant, draft, or other source where tenders reload.
A pumper (or tender/pumper) that stays and supplies the attack engine while others shuttle.
Usable tank gallons minus the reserve you refuse to burn.

safetyNotes: Dump sites and fill sites are vehicle, drop-off, and drowning hazards. Spotters and lighting matter at night.
Do not dump into a collapsing tank or onto charged hose.
Traffic control is part of water supply. A wrecked tender is zero GPM.
If tank water is about to die, the officer needs that sentence immediately — interior crews are using water they think they have.

drill.objective: Plan a rural water supply: tank duration, shuttle or relay choice, fill/dump jobs, and the radio loop before the tank hits reserve.
drill.equipment: Engine tank figure, radios, tender/shuttle calculator, map or cones for fill and dump, optional portable tank.
drill.setup: Tabletop is enough if you cannot move tenders. Assign attack pump, dump-site boss, and at least one tender driver. State the stop signal.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: Given tank size and a fire flow, compute working time with a reserve. Name fill site, dump site, and the first radio sentence when time is short.
commonMistakes: Calling every truck a ‘tanker’ with no job
Waiting until the tank is empty to talk
debrief: How many minutes of working water do we have?
Who do we call first for more water?

15.title: 15-minute shuttle plan
15.instructions: Use the tender calculators to build a cycle: fill, dump, travel, tender count, target GPM. Compare to tank duration. Decide shuttle vs draft/relay. Brief the radio words.
commonMistakes: Counting tenders that have not been given a fill site
debrief: What step in the cycle is the bottleneck?
When would we switch to a relay or a second fill site?

30.title: 30-minute rural scenario
30.instructions: Run or tabletop a working fire: initial tank attack, first tender dump, a fill-site delay inject, then a flow increase. Operator must keep tank duration honest and say when the shuttle cannot meet demand. Include a portable-tank or nurse decision.
commonMistakes: Tenders circling with no dump site
Raising fire flow with no water math
debrief: What would make you tell the officer to cut flow?
How do we keep one tender from blocking the dump site?

readinessQuestions.q: The most useful first rural-water question on arrival is:
choices: How shiny are the tenders?
How long will this tank last at the flow we are about to use, and what is the next water?
What is static hydrant pressure in town?
Should we wait to stretch until every tender arrives?
readinessQuestions.why: Tank duration plus a next-water plan is the rural clock.

readinessQuestions.q: Shuttle flow goes up most honestly when you:
choices: Count every apparatus on the printout as a working tender
Shorten real cycle time or add tenders that can actually complete the loop
Open a second attack line with no dump site
Idle the fill site to ‘save the hydrant’
readinessQuestions.why: GPM is gallons that finish the cycle, divided by minutes. Fantasy units do not dump.

readinessQuestions.q: If fill time doubles because the fill site is poorly staffed, shuttle GPM will:
choices: Stay the same because travel did not change
Fall, because cycle time got longer
Double
Only affect the attack engine’s intake color
readinessQuestions.why: Every slow step is in the denominator.

readinessQuestions.q: The officer should hear that tank water is short:
choices: At the critique
As soon as working time will not cover the next stretch of the fire
Only after the pump sucks air
Never — handle it on the panel
readinessQuestions.why: Interior decisions assume water that may already be gone.

skills.title: Apparatus Placement
skills.summary: Stop the engine where the hose, water, rescue path, later units, and a way out all still work — then set the brake and own that decision.
skills.whyItMatters: A bad spot is a permanent tactical problem. You can recut a line. You cannot un-park a blocked aerial or a hydrant you drove past with no plan.
learningPoints: Placement is a size-up skill: occupancy, fire location, access, water, collapse/overhead, and who is coming after you.
First engine usually owns a working spot for attack and water — not the front door selfie. Leave the aerial, ambulance, and later engines a path.
Hydrant vs fire: know whether this department lays in, lays out, or spots at the building and waits for water. Do not invent a third method in the driveway.
Once the parking brake is set, you still own wheel chocks, pump engagement setup, and a way to move if command orders it.
Say the placement out loud if it is non-obvious: ‘taking the hydrant side, leaving the front for the truck.’
beforeYouDo: Know first-due hose loads, LDH, and whether you are expected to hit a hydrant before the building.
Know typical later-arriving apparatus for this alarm (truck, rescue, second engine) and what they need.
Have a backup spot if the driveway, wires, or parked cars steal the textbook position.

terminology.meaning: A position that lets this company do its job without stealing the next company’s job.
Department water-supply driving pattern — hydrant first vs building first. Follow yours.
Area to keep clear of people and apparatus if the building or wall can come down.
A way to get this rig or later rigs out — not a dead-end jammed with hose.

safetyNotes: Do not spot under wires, dying walls, or on known collapse sides just to be close.
Never leave the apparatus in drive on a grade. Brake, chock, and follow department wheel-chock rules.
Personnel in the street while you spot: the hydrant firefighter and later units. Slow is part of the skill.
Do not block hydrants, FDCs, or the only aerial corner because the address felt urgent.

drill.objective: Choose and defend an engine spot for three different arrivals, including water, later units, and a way out.
drill.equipment: Printed or projected arrival photos, cones or a parking lot, radios, department hose/hydrant SOP.
drill.setup: No live pumping required. Use photos first, then walk a station apron or training lot if available. Officer or instructor plays later-arriving truck.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: From one photo, point to where this engine stops, where the hydrant or FDC is, and what you left for the truck. Say it in one radio sentence.
commonMistakes: Nose on the front door with no water story
debrief: What would make you take a worse-looking spot that is actually better?
Who is coming after us?

15.title: 15-minute three-spot tabletop
15.instructions: Three scenes: house fire with a hydrant past the address, garden apartment narrow lane, and a standpipe building. Operator spots each, then the instructor steals one option (parked car, wires, blocked hydrant). Adjust without losing water or later access.
performancePoints: Adjustment when the first choice dies
commonMistakes: Hydrant forgotten until the line is dry
debrief: Which scene would you hydrant first?
What do you tell command if you cannot get the textbook spot?

30.title: 30-minute lot or scenario
30.instructions: On a training lot or with cones, spot for attack, then a second engine and a truck arrive. Include a ‘move up’ order and a hose that will trap you if you dump it in the only egress. Debrief with the decision sim on a similar occupancy.
commonMistakes: Final parking wherever the bumper stopped
Arguing instead of taking the next best hole
debrief: When is a farther spot the safer pump position?
How do we move if command needs the hole?

readinessQuestions.q: A good first-engine spot is one that:
choices: Looks closest to the fire in the windshield
Lets this company work water and hose while leaving a path for later units and a way out
Blocks the driveway so nobody else can mess it up
Always sits on the address side regardless of hydrant or wires
readinessQuestions.why: You are parking a water-and-hose platform inside a larger incident, not winning a closeness contest.

readinessQuestions.q: If the only close spot sits under wires on a working fire side, the operator should:
choices: Take it anyway because seconds matter more than overhead
Choose the next working spot that does not put the crew and rig under that hazard, and say so
Wait in the street with the pump in road
Park on the sidewalk and leave the brake off
readinessQuestions.why: A burned windshield is slower than fifty extra feet of hose from a survivable hole.

readinessQuestions.q: Department lay-in / lay-out / hydrant-then-building patterns exist so that:
choices: Every driver can freelance
Water and hose get to the fire the way this agency trained
The aerial always has to wait
You never need a hydrant firefighter
readinessQuestions.why: Placement and water supply are one SOP. Do not invent a third pattern in the dark.

readinessQuestions.q: After the brake is set, apparatus placement is:
choices: Finished forever
Still your problem if command needs the hole, hose traps the rig, or the spot is unsafe
The officer’s alone
Only about how it photographs
readinessQuestions.why: You can be asked to move. Chocks, hose, and a remaining path make that possible.

skills.title: Pump and Supply Troubleshooting
skills.summary: Change one variable at a time: supply, valves, air, restrictions, cavitation, governor, then the discharge side.
skills.whyItMatters: Panic makes operators twist everything. Method makes water come back.
learningPoints: Start with: do I have water at the pump?
Then: is a valve wrong?
Then: is the pump cavitating or out of prime?
Then: is the problem on the discharge/hose/nozzle side?
Tell the officer what you know, not a novel.
beforeYouDo: Know the panel well enough to find tank-to-pump, intakes, and discharges in the dark.
Keep a light and a hydrant wrench where you always keep them.

terminology.meaning: Kink, closed gate, debris, or a weak source starving the pump.
Closed gate, kink, burst, or nozzle issue after the pump.

safetyNotes: Do not stand over charged lines while ‘fixing’ blindly.
A burst LDH is a violent event.

drill.objective: Diagnose three seeded problems using a one-variable-at-a-time method and a short radio report.
drill.equipment: Pump panel or training cards, radios, optional live pump.
drill.setup: Instructor seeds: closed intake, kink, wrong discharge, weak residual, or primer issue.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: Recite the order: water at pump → valves → cavitation/prime → discharge.
debrief: What is your first gauge glance?

15.title: 15-minute cards
15.instructions: Three scenario cards. Operator states first check and the radio sentence.
debrief: What did you tell command?

30.title: 30-minute live or panel
30.instructions: Seeded faults on an authorized evolution or a full tabletop with time pressure.
performancePoints: Crew not left dry without a warning
debrief: How fast should the officer hear there is a water problem?

readinessQuestions.q: Best first question when a line goes soft:
choices: Is the radio on scan?
Do I still have water at the pump (intake/tank) and an open path to that discharge?
Should I add foam?
Should I pull a second engine immediately without looking?
readinessQuestions.why: Locate the failure. Supply and valves first.

readinessQuestions.q: Changing several controls at once is a problem because:
choices: It looks decisive
You cannot tell what actually fixed or broke the situation
Pumps require it
Officers prefer it
readinessQuestions.why: One variable at a time is how you learn and how you recover.

readinessQuestions.q: The officer needs to hear a water problem:
choices: At the critique tomorrow
As soon as you know attack water is in doubt
Only if the tank is empty
Never — handle it quietly
readinessQuestions.why: Interior crews make life decisions based on water they think they have.
